mSDT: Multi-Item Signal Detection Theory

Colin G. Tredoux

Tamsyn M. Naylor

2026-10-30

Source: vignettes/msdt_model.Rmd
msdt_model.Rmd

Acknowledgement. Large language models supplied by Anthropic and OpenAI were used in preparing this vignette, to assist with checking code, testing the veracity of the approaches described, and on occasion editing the text. Responsibility for the content rests with the authors.

Overview

This vignette introduces core utilities for the multi-item signal detection theory (mSDT) model of Yang, Burke and Healy (2025), covering the components that are mathematically well defined under equal variance and independent filler signals.

library(r4lineups)

What mSDT offers over ordinary SDT

Signal detection theory was built for a binary decision: one item is presented, the observer says “old” or “new”, and sensitivity is the separation between two distributions. It works because there is exactly one signal to evaluate against one criterion.

A lineup is not that. The witness sees m items at once and has three kinds of response available: identify the suspect, identify a filler, or reject the lineup. Classical SDT has no natural place for the filler identification — it is neither a hit nor a correct rejection — and the usual workarounds either discard filler choices or fold them into an error rate, which throws away the most diagnostic information the lineup produces.

mSDT accommodates them by changing what is modelled. Instead of one signal, it models the joint distribution of the suspect’s signal and the strongest filler’s signal. Every response then follows from a single decision rule: if the largest signal in the lineup fails to reach the criterion the witness rejects; otherwise they choose whichever member produced it. Suspect identifications, filler identifications and rejections all fall out of the same model, which is what classical SDT cannot do.

If signal detection theory itself is unfamiliar, the “Signal Detection Theory, briefly” section of vignette("simulation_power_analysis") sets out discriminability and criterion without assuming background, and vignette("sdt_glm_analysis") shows how the binary case relates to ordinary regression.

The model is set out in full in Yang, Burke and Healy (2025), which is open access — see the References below.

Key components implemented here:

  • The max filler distribution for m−1m - 1 independent standard normal fillers
  • Parameter estimation from rejection rates in culprit-absent and culprit-present lineups (equivalently, target-absent and target-present)
  • Joint distribution visualisation (suspect signal against max filler signal)

Joint distributions, and whether fillers are independent

A univariate distribution describes one quantity — how likely the suspect’s signal is to take each value. A joint distribution describes two or more together, including how they move with one another.

The distinction matters here because the witness’s decision is not about the suspect’s signal in isolation. It is about whether the suspect’s signal is the largest and clears the criterion. That is inherently a question about two quantities at once, so a joint distribution is the natural object.

The models implemented here assume the filler signals are independent of one another. That assumption is convenient — it is what makes the max-filler distribution a simple power of the normal CDF — but it is not obviously true. Fillers in a real lineup are chosen to match a description, so they resemble each other. A witness whose memory happens to align with that description may find all of them somewhat familiar, and one whose memory does not may find none of them familiar. That is precisely what correlation means.

The consequence is not small. Under independence the largest of five standard normal fillers has an expected value of about 1.17. If the fillers are strongly correlated the shared component dominates and the maximum is much less extreme — around 0.37 at a correlation of 0.9, roughly a third of the independent value. Treating correlated fillers as independent therefore overstates how often a filler out-competes the suspect, and so understates the suspect’s exposure. The implementation plan below treats this as the first extension worth building.

Max filler distribution

Because the witness responds to whichever member feels strongest, the quantity that decides the outcome is not any particular filler’s signal but the largest of them. So the distribution needed is that of the maximum of m−1m-1 filler signals.

Under independence it has a simple closed form. The maximum is below xx exactly when every filler is below xx, so

P(max⁡<x)=Φ(x)m−1 P(\max < x) = \Phi(x)^{m-1}

and the density follows by differentiating. This is the whole reason the independence assumption is attractive.

dmax_filler(0, lineup_size = 6)   # density at 0
#> [1] 0.1246695
pmax_filler(0, lineup_size = 6)   # P(max filler < 0) = 0.5^5
#> [1] 0.03125
qmax_filler(0.5, lineup_size = 6) # median of the max filler signal
#> [1] 1.128998

Note that pmax_filler(0, lineup_size = 6) is 0.03125, which is 0.550.5^5: with five fillers, all five must fall below zero.

The practical point is that the max filler distribution is shifted well to the right of the distribution of any single filler. Each filler is centred at 0, but the largest of five is centred near 1.17. A culprit with d′=1d' = 1 is therefore competing against a typical best-filler signal higher than its own mean — which is why lineup identification is hard, and why lineup size matters so much.

Moments

A moment is a summary number describing the shape of a distribution. The three used here are the familiar ones under formal names: the first moment is the mean, which says where the distribution sits; the second central moment is the variance, which says how spread out it is; and the third standardised moment is the skewness, which says how asymmetric it is — zero for a symmetric distribution, positive when the right tail is longer.

They matter here because the max filler distribution is not normal, even though every filler individually is. Taking a maximum shifts the distribution right, compresses its spread, and makes it asymmetric. The moments quantify exactly that, and they are computed numerically because no simple closed form exists.

moments <- max_filler_moments(6)

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Moment = c("Mean", "Variance", "Skewness"),
    Value  = round(c(moments$mean, moments$var, moments$skewness), 4),
    Reading = c("Centre: well above the 0 of any single filler",
                "Spread: narrower than a single filler's variance of 1",
                "Asymmetry: positive, so a longer right tail")
  ),
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Moments of the maximum of five independent standard normal filler signals (lineup size 6). Analytic quantities, not computed from data."
)
Moments of the maximum of five independent standard normal filler signals (lineup size 6). Analytic quantities, not computed from data.
Moment Value Reading
Mean 1.1630 Centre: well above the 0 of any single filler
Variance 0.4475 Spread: narrower than a single filler’s variance of 1
Skewness 0.3026 Asymmetry: positive, so a longer right tail

Estimating mSDT parameters from rejection rates

Let

  • Pr⁡(REJ∣I)\Pr(\mathrm{REJ}\mid I) be the rejection rate in culprit-absent lineups
  • Pr⁡(REJ∣G)\Pr(\mathrm{REJ}\mid G) be the rejection rate in culprit-present lineups

Then (Yang et al., 2025):

Pr⁡(REJ∣I)=Φ(γ)m,Pr⁡(REJ∣G)=Φ(γ−d′)Φ(γ)m−1 \Pr(\mathrm{REJ}\mid I) = \Phi(\gamma)^m, \qquad \Pr(\mathrm{REJ}\mid G) = \Phi(\gamma - d')\,\Phi(\gamma)^{m-1}

Why rejection rates in particular

Because they are the one outcome with a clean algebraic form, and between them they identify both parameters.

A rejection occurs only when every signal in the lineup falls below the criterion. In a culprit-absent lineup all mm members are fillers, so the rejection rate is Φ(γ)m\Phi(\gamma)^m — and note what is absent from that expression: d′d'. The culprit-absent rejection rate depends on the criterion alone, so it pins γ\gamma down by itself.

In a culprit-present lineup the culprit must fall below the criterion and so must the m−1m-1 fillers, giving Φ(γ−d′)Φ(γ)m−1\Phi(\gamma - d')\Phi(\gamma)^{m-1}. With γ\gamma already known from the first equation, the gap between the two rejection rates fixes d′d'.

Two equations, two unknowns, solved in closed form — no optimiser, no starting values, no convergence to check. That is the appeal.

What the helper does

estimate_msdt_params() is a convenience function that performs that algebra for you: it inverts the first equation for γ\gamma, substitutes into the second, and inverts for d′d'. The two steps are also available separately as msdt_gamma_from_rej() and msdt_dprime_from_rej().

params <- estimate_msdt_params(pr_rej_I = 0.25, pr_rej_G = 0.15,
                               lineup_size = 6)
params
#> $gamma
#> [1] 0.8193286
#> 
#> $dprime
#> [1] 0.8789708
# The estimate reproduces the input rejection rate exactly, as it must
pnorm(params$gamma)^6
#> [1] 0.25

What this estimator gives up

The closed form comes at a price, and it is worth stating plainly.

estimate_msdt_params() uses only the two rejection rates. It never looks at whether the witnesses who did choose picked the suspect or a filler. Since a suspect identification and a filler identification carry very different evidential weight, that is a great deal of information to leave on the table — arguably the most informative part of the data.

The estimator is also exactly identified: two numbers in, two parameters out, with nothing left over. There is no residual, so there is no goodness-of-fit test. The model cannot be found to fit badly, because it will always reproduce the two rates it was given exactly.

Use it when the rejection rates are all you have, or as a quick starting point. Where the full response breakdown exists, prefer:

Function Uses Gives you
estimate_msdt_params() Two rejection rates γ\gamma and d′d', closed form, no fit statistic
fit_max_sdt() All suspect/filler/reject counts d′d' and criterion, plus a chi-square goodness-of-fit and bootstrap intervals
fit_winter_2ht() All suspect/filler/reject counts A different process account, separating detection from guessing and bias

fit_max_sdt() fits the same MAX decision rule as here, on the compound decision structure described by Duncan (2006), by minimising Pearson chi-square rather than maximising a likelihood. See vignette("model_comparison") for the 2-HT alternative.

Joint distribution plots

These show the decision space directly: the suspect’s signal on one axis, the strongest filler’s signal on the other. The MAX rule carves that plane into three regions — reject, identify the suspect, identify a filler — and the contours show where the probability mass falls in each.

plot_msdt_joint(dprime = 1.2, gamma = 0.4, lineup_size = 6,
                lineup_type = "culprit_present")

plot_msdt_joint(dprime = 1.2, gamma = 0.4, lineup_size = 6,
                lineup_type = "culprit_absent")

These plots use no dataset. They are analytic densities drawn from the parameters supplied in the call — here d′=1.2d' = 1.2, γ=0.4\gamma = 0.4 and a six-person lineup — not summaries of observed data. Comparing the two makes the model’s logic visible: in the culprit-absent plot the mass sits symmetrically about the diagonal, since the suspect is just another filler; in the culprit-present plot it is displaced by d′d' towards the suspect axis.

Planned extensions

The functions here implement the core mSDT assumptions: equal variance and independent filler signals. Yang et al. (2025) discuss extensions that are not yet implemented. Rather than leave that as a bare caveat, here is what each would take.

1. Correlated filler signals

Why it matters. As noted above, fillers matched to a common description are unlikely to be independent, and the error runs in an unsafe direction: assuming independence overstates the competition the suspect faces.

How to implement it. Equicorrelated fillers admit a one-factor representation. Writing ρ\rho for the common correlation,

fi=ρZ+1−ρei f_i = \sqrt{\rho}\,Z + \sqrt{1-\rho}\,e_i

with ZZ and the eie_i independent standard normals. Conditional on ZZ the fillers are independent, so the existing power-of-Φ\Phi result applies inside an expectation over ZZ:

P(max⁡<x)=∫ϕ(z)Φ(x−ρz1−ρ)m−1dz P(\max < x) = \int \phi(z)\, \Phi\!\left(\frac{x - \sqrt{\rho}\,z}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}\right)^{m-1} dz

a one-dimensional integral, evaluable with stats::integrate(). This extends dmax_filler() and friends by a single rho argument defaulting to 0, which reduces exactly to the current behaviour.

Effort: small. Risk: low — the formula is checkable against simulation, and ρ=0\rho = 0 must reproduce the existing functions.

2. Unequal variances

Why it matters. The empirical evidence in recognition memory generally favours a culprit distribution with larger variance than the filler distribution, and assuming equality distorts d′d'.

The obstacle is identifiability, not arithmetic. With a culprit signal N(d′,σ2)N(d', \sigma^2) the rejection rates become

Pr⁡(REJ∣I)=Φ(γ)m,Pr⁡(REJ∣G)=Φ(γ−d′σ)Φ(γ)m−1 \Pr(\mathrm{REJ}\mid I) = \Phi(\gamma)^m, \qquad \Pr(\mathrm{REJ}\mid G) = \Phi\!\left(\frac{\gamma - d'}{\sigma}\right)\Phi(\gamma)^{m-1}

which is two equations in three unknowns. σ\sigma is simply not identified from rejection rates, so estimate_msdt_params() cannot be extended to cover it. The extension belongs in fit_max_sdt(), which uses the full response breakdown, or requires confidence data and the z-ROC slope (fit_sdt_roc()).

Effort: moderate. Risk: higher — the third parameter must be shown to be recoverable before the option is offered, which means a simulation study sweeping σ\sigma and sample size and checking recovery, on the model of the identifiability concerns raised in vignette("lineup_memory_models").

3. Order of work

Correlated fillers first: it is self-contained, verifiable against simulation, and backwards compatible. Unequal variance second, and only after a recovery study establishes that the parameter can be estimated at realistic sample sizes. Shipping an option that returns an unidentified parameter would be worse than not shipping it.

Technical Details

What is computed

Function Quantity Form
dmax_filler() Density of the max of m−1m-1 fillers (m−1)ϕ(x)Φ(x)m−2(m-1)\phi(x)\Phi(x)^{m-2}
pmax_filler() CDF Φ(x)m−1\Phi(x)^{m-1}
qmax_filler() Quantile Φ−1(p1/(m−1))\Phi^{-1}(p^{1/(m-1)})
max_filler_moments() Mean, variance, skewness Numerical integration
estimate_msdt_params() γ\gamma, d′d' Closed form from the two rejection rates

Assumptions

  1. Filler signals are independent and identically distributed N(0,1)N(0, 1). See the planned extension above for the correlated case.
  2. The culprit signal is N(d′,1)N(d', 1) — equal variance.
  3. A single criterion γ\gamma is applied to the largest signal, with no confidence criteria.
  4. Lineups are simultaneous and fair, so lineup_size counts functioning alternatives. A lineup with null foils has a smaller effective size than its nominal size, and since mm enters the equations directly, both γ\gamma and d′d' will be biased. Check lineup_table() first.
  5. estimate_msdt_params() is exactly identified and therefore untestable — no residual, no goodness-of-fit.

References

Duncan, M. (2006). A signal detection model of compound decision tasks (Technical Note DRDC TR 2006-256). Defence R&D Canada, Toronto.

Wixted, J. T., Vul, E., Mickes, L., & Wilson, B. M. (2018). Models of lineup memory. Cognitive Psychology, 105, 81-114.

Yang, Y., Burke, J. L., & Healy, J. (2025). A multi-item signal detection theory model for eyewitness identification. Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications, 10, 54.
